body:
Turn arithmetic into a timed experiment

Purpose. Identify the compiler’s output: a legal measurement schedule, rather than only a list of arithmetic gates.

A register wire may represent many logical qubits. An \(n\)-bit adder preserves its first operand and wraps its second modulo \(2^n\); \(a\) below counts clean work qubits. A circuit contract must preserve relative phases as well as computational-basis values.

Section VIII produces a logical measurement schedule: where the qubits live, which measurements overlap, and when factories can supply another state. Architecture primitives later turn that schedule into ion transport and physical gates.

Arithmetic

Which reversible map? Count Toffolis.

Schedule

Which operations can overlap? Count measurement layers.

Device

Which encoded blocks and factories? Count physical qubits.

Keep the interface fixed; change the implementation

Purpose. Separate what an operation must compute from the circuit chosen to implement it, enabling safe substitutions.

A spec states the public map; a def decomposes it. For addition,

\[U_{\rm add}|x,y\rangle=|x,x+y\bmod 2^n\rangle,\qquad V_{\rm def}|x,y,0^a\rangle=(U_{\rm add}|x,y\rangle)|0^a\rangle.\]

The second equation requires the implementation to erase its clean workspace. Measurement-based definitions must satisfy it after outcome-dependent corrections. Ripple carry and carry lookahead can share this interface while having different placement and timing costs.

The contract exposes what matters

Purpose. Use a small contract to show which input, output and phase properties an implementation must preserve.

Visible to the callerChosen by the implementation
Input and output registers; arithmetic modulusCarry workspace; gate decomposition; qubit placement
Correct amplitudes and phases; clean work on returnMeasurement outcomes and their correction records

Structure carries scheduling information

Purpose. Retain arithmetic hierarchy so placement and scheduling can exploit structure instead of treating every gate independently.

A point addition contains lookups, differences, division, square subtraction, and multiplication. Keeping these boundaries exposes useful lifetimes: division can release history storage for the next adder; a constant can be loaded into spare positions and added as a register. The compiler then lowers every selected leaf to an architecture-supported instruction. Hierarchy guides the choices; the final schedule demonstrates that they fit.

A frame update changes the next measurement

Purpose. Explain how deferred Clifford operations change later measurement questions rather than disappearing from the computation.

The instructions are Pauli measurements, tracked Clifford operations, and resource-state consumption. For result \(m\), a Pauli measurement applies

\[\Pi_m(P)=\frac{I+(-1)^mP}{2},\qquad \Pi_m(P)C=C\Pi_m(C^\dagger PC).\]

Thus a Clifford \(C\) can move into the software frame if later measurement observables change with it. The drawing makes the physical consequence visible: moving target-Z measurement through CNOT changes one-qubit support into two-qubit ZZ support. That new support must still be legal, and accumulated frames eventually need clearing.

What “end-to-end” includes

Purpose. Clarify which preparation, routing and correction operations must be included before a schedule is called end-to-end.

The authors compile major components separately, connect their layouts through an authored routing sequence, and charge 20 extra layers per point-addition window. This supports a composable schedule estimate, without establishing a globally optimal monolithic circuit. Appendix D gives the lowering machinery; table lookup supplies the specifically borrowed zipper and movement constructions.

summary: The paper connects arithmetic circuits to executable logical measurements through a structured compiler. Preserving operation contracts and layouts makes scheduling and routing costs explicit. This is the bridge between a gate count and the hardware runtime estimate.
title: VIII · From arithmetic to executable measurements

body:
A layer must pass two tests

Purpose. Distinguish algebraic permission to overlap operations from the availability of the physical resources they require.

A Q102 block encodes 22 logical qubits in 102 data qubits. A cat is an entangled ancilla used to measure a Pauli product. CCZ means controlled-controlled-Z; its prepared three-qubit state supplies the corresponding non-Clifford gate.

Operations must be causally movable and physically compatible. The target has 69 Q102 memory blocks, each storing 22 logical qubits. Its headline per-layer limits are:

ResourceLimitWhat the count omits
Logical measurements per block3Pauli-support and frame compatibility
Memory-side cat-bundle pairs24 totalWhich blocks each bundle must touch
CCZ injection1Factory readiness and subsequent cleanup

Assigning measurement \(j\) a layer \(\ell_j\) must respect \(\ell_j>\ell_i\) for a strict dependency \(i\prec j\). Commutation alone does not guarantee that two measurements fit the same hardware layer.

Earlier measurement, changed observable

Purpose. Derive how a measurement observable changes when moved across an earlier operation.

For a Hermitian Pauli \(P\), \(\Pi_m(P)=(I+(-1)^mP)/2\) projects onto eigenvalue \((-1)^m\). \(c,t\) label CNOT control and target; \(C\) is the Clifford.

\[\Pi_m(P)C=C\Pi_m(C^\dagger PC),\qquad C^\dagger Z_tC=Z_cZ_t\quad(C=\mathrm{CNOT}).\]

Moving a measurement backward through a Clifford changes its support. The scheduler must recheck physical compatibility at the new position.

A missing sign can wait

Purpose. Allow early measurement when the unresolved correction only changes how its outcome is interpreted.

\[\Pi_m(Z)X^s=X^s\Pi_{m\oplus s}(Z).\]

If \(s\) is unresolved, measure Z now and store the logical result as “raw bit XOR \(s\).” Such expressions are the scheduler's virtual measurement values.

A missing basis cannot wait

Purpose. Identify a genuine dependency when the unresolved correction changes which observable must be measured.

Pending correctionRequired observableConsequence
\(X^s\)\((-1)^sZ\)Same measurement; interpret its sign later
\(H^s\)Z if \(s=0\); X if \(s=1\)Basis changes; wait for \(s\)

An anticommuting earlier measurement also blocks motion: exchanging X and Z measurements changes the experiment.

Algorithm 1: scan backward, stop at a real obstacle

Purpose. Turn the commutation and resource conditions into a scheduling procedure that stops at an actual dependency.

Starting from a serially valid position, propagate the observable backward through Clifford updates, revise outcome expressions, and test each candidate layer. Stop at the causal floor or a blocking dependency; commit the earliest legal position found. This greedy procedure supplies a realizable depth under the model, with no claim of global optimality.

Two different reasons to stall

Purpose. Separate waiting for an unknown measurement basis from waiting for an occupied hardware resource.

Resource stall

Two independent CCZ injections still occupy separate layers: the injection port is shared.

Basis stall

A measurement whose basis depends on an unresolved bit must wait, even with idle ports.

Commutation becomes a parity test

Purpose. Evaluate Pauli commutation efficiently through binary parity calculations used by the scheduler.

Represent a Pauli, ignoring overall phase, by \(P(x,z)=X^xZ^z\), with binary vectors \(x,z\). Then

\[P(x,z)P(x',z')=(-1)^{x\cdot z'+z\cdot x'}P(x',z')P(x,z).\]

Two local anticommutations cancel: \(X_1X_2\) commutes with \(Z_1Z_2\), while \(X_1\) does not. Block-local bitmasks make this support test cheap across the enormous instruction stream.
summary: This section explains the compiler’s scheduling rules. Commutation permits some measurements to move earlier, but unresolved bases and finite hardware resources still impose delays. The improvement is greater legal overlap without changing the logical computation.
title: IX · Scheduling with Pauli frames and finite resources

body:
Arrange qubits so corrections stay local

Purpose. Choose layouts that keep correction operations local before attempting to overlap communication with arithmetic.

Here Q102 is the \([[102,22,9]]\) memory code. Each \(x_i,y_i,c_i\) is a logical bit: two operands and carry workspace. A Clifford frame is a classically tracked operation; it changes how later Pauli measurements are interpreted.

A Q102 block holds seven operand/work triples \((x_i,y_i,c_i)\) plus one carry relay. Across 37 blocks this forms a 256-bit adder lane. Most CNOT and CZ corrections then remain within a block and can be tracked in its Clifford frame. Only boundary carries need relaying.

Serial arithmetic can win when its moving carry wave matches the machine's cheap local operations.

A move is a parity measurement plus cleanup

Purpose. Implement movement through parity measurement and feedforward so it can fit the architecture’s measurement primitives.

Operation and correctionState after correction
Start\((\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle)_s|+\rangle_d\)
Measure \(Z_sZ_d\to a\); apply \(X_d^a\)\(\alpha|00\rangle+\beta|11\rangle\)
Measure \(X_s\to b\); apply \(Z_d^b\)\((\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle)_d\)

The intermediate “copy” is an entangled encoding of one state. Measuring the source completes the move; its phase correction can remain in software.

Distribute a control; erase by parity

Purpose. Distribute one control across several locations without leaving uncontrolled phases when its copies are erased.

One XX layer prepares Bell links; a ZZ layer joins them to the source, producing \(\alpha|0\cdots0\rangle+\beta|1\cdots1\rangle\) after corrections. Measuring spare copies in X leaves correction \(Z^{b_1\oplus\cdots\oplus b_r}\) on the retained qubit.

In this drawing the receiving pairs carry offsets \(s_1\) and \(s_1\oplus s_2\); the displayed X corrections remove them. Placement and cat availability determine whether these two layers fit. Spare local positions also let two remote moves implement a swap in parallel.

Figure 2 shows the generic remote-gate construction that tailored placement avoids repeating for every arithmetic CNOT and CZ.

Use the disappearing carry as a routing opportunity

Purpose. Use workspace released by the carry computation to move data while the adder is still executing.

\[p=2^{256}-c,\quad c=2^{32}+977,\qquad x+y=s+q2^{256}\equiv s+qc\pmod p.\]

The full addition is followed by a 65-bit correction and a high-32-bit phase comparator. Canonical reduction and rare boundary failures require the separate Appendix B analysis.

Full carry-out addition

Finish each block's reverse ripple; immediately release its work positions.

Small correction

Park low source bits; fan out the carry; load \(qc\); run the 65-bit adder.

Close the layout

Erase the loaded constant, restore parked bits, and repair measurement phases.

Routing almost disappears from the serial path

Purpose. Compare the routed depth with the arithmetic’s serial requirement to quantify how much movement was hidden.

\[\underbrace{510}_{\text{full adder}}+\underbrace{128}_{\text{small adder}}+\underbrace{31}_{\text{unhidden comparison}}=669,\qquad D_{\rm compiled}=674.\]

The five extra layers fit inside the separately modeled CliNR seam delay of roughly 7.73 layers. Charging both that delay and another five-layer penalty would double count the same waiting. Up to three compatible measurements per block allow rearrangement behind the carry wave.

The same rule governs the whole window

Purpose. Apply the same placement-and-overlap strategy to the other components of a complete point-addition window.

Zipper lookup overlaps two 15-bit traversals; shrinking gcd registers release space for output and compressed history; square subtraction shifts products during arithmetic. Peak usage is 68 active blocks plus the index block. Appendix C closes the full placement loop; composition charges 20 extra routing layers per window.
summary: The paper overlaps data movement with arithmetic instead of adding a separate routing stage. Carefully chosen layouts and measurement-based moves hide most routing depth, at the cost of respecting block-local correction and resource constraints.
title: X · Moving data while arithmetic is already running

body:
Correct arithmetic and executable scheduling are separate claims

Purpose. Separate the claim that a circuit computes correctly from the claim that its measurement schedule can run on the device.

Use \(X,Y,Z\) for Pauli gates, \(H\) for Hadamard, and \(\lvert+\rangle=(\lvert0\rangle+\lvert1\rangle)/\sqrt2\). Measurement bit \(m\) records eigenvalue \((-1)^m\); \(\oplus\) is XOR. A cat bundle is the ancilla hardware for a Pauli-product measurement.

The checker must verify both the quantum map and the hardware restrictions. A legal resource schedule can still contain a wrong phase; correct arithmetic can still demand unavailable cat bundles.

Choose a contract that sees the possible bug

Purpose. Choose a verification contract that includes the kind of error the circuit could introduce, including relative phases.

ContractWhat it recordsTypical use
Basis\(|x\rangle\mapsto|f(x)\rangle\)Reversible arithmetic labels
Basis plus phase\(|x\rangle\mapsto e^{i\theta(x)}|f(x)\rangle\)Phase-aware arithmetic and cleanup
Full operatorGeneral quantum evolution, including corrected measurement branchesSmall quantum primitives

Identity and Z preserve the same basis labels but send \(|+\rangle\) to different states. Basis labels alone cannot establish coherent correctness.

Erasing a work bit leaves a visible phase

Purpose. Demonstrate why correct basis values are insufficient when measurement-based cleanup leaves an input-dependent sign.

\[\sum_{a,b}\alpha_{ab}|a,b,0\rangle\xrightarrow{\text{compute AND}}\sum_{a,b}\alpha_{ab}|a,b,ab\rangle\xrightarrow{M_X\to m}\sum_{a,b}\alpha_{ab}(-1)^{mab}|a,b\rangle.\]

The last state is normalized after conditioning on the outcome. A conditional \(CZ^m\) cancels the phase.

CaseMeasurement phaseCorrectionNet phase
\(mab=0\)\(+1\)\(+1\)\(+1\)
\(m=a=b=1\)\(-1\)\(-1\)\(+1\)

The transparent compute-AND circuit exposes the cleanup identity; an optimized injection can implement its compute step differently.

Prove the parent from its children

Purpose. Use verified component contracts to justify replacing a parent operation with its implementation.

\[V_r\cdots V_1|x\rangle|0\rangle_A=(U_{\rm spec}|x\rangle)|0\rangle_A.\]

Here \(V_1,\ldots,V_r\) are child operations, \(U_{\rm spec}\) is the parent map, and \(A\) is workspace, not a curve point. The checker binds public registers to internal locations, composes child contracts, checks their input domains, and checks every promised clean work qubit. This proves the parent only to the extent that the child contracts hold on all inputs they receive.

Testing cannot certify rare approximation failures

Purpose. Explain why ordinary test samples cannot resolve the very small failure probabilities used in the analysis.

The authors report 100,000 reproducibly sampled input pairs for the secp256k1 approximate adder, plus tests at other widths. For a bug of probability \(\varepsilon\) under the test distribution, its chance of escaping \(N\) independent tests is \((1-\varepsilon)^N\). Rare or unsampled cases can survive. Section IV and Appendix B instead bound the specified approximations mathematically.

Check the failure mode with the right experiment

Purpose. Match each scheduling or implementation risk to a check capable of detecting that failure.

Reported checkWhat it can catch
Basis simulation of the 674-layer adderWrong arithmetic
Reduced-scale phase-aware and superposition testsWrong relative phases
Cat, injection, block, and routing validationIllegal parallelism or unavailable resources
Analytic cost envelopes and small full programsMissing work and composition errors

What remains necessary for independent reproduction

Purpose. Identify the additional implementation details needed to independently reproduce the compiled estimate.

A declared run records parameters, architecture, layout, code versions, schedule, metrics, and check results. Recounting a saved schedule is easier than rebuilding the compiler. The paper describes these retained artifacts; its prose is not the executable component library. These notes have not independently rerun the internal compiler or noise simulations.
summary: This section explains what the compiler’s checks establish and what they do not. Arithmetic correctness, phase correctness and schedule legality require different tests; finite sampling alone cannot certify extremely rare approximation failures.
title: XI · What the compiler checks, and what those checks prove

body:
Follow the register's meaning as well as its location

Purpose. Explain how to read a layout whose qubits change both position and arithmetic role during execution.

This page uses \(P,Q\) for the two points being added, not specifically the public generator and key. Set \(R=P+Q\). All coordinate operations are modulo \(p=2^{256}-2^{32}-977\); the formulas assume the nonexceptional affine branch.

Figure 21 closes a full point-addition window: packed coordinate storage becomes an interleaved arithmetic lane, serves several algebraic roles, and returns to its entry layout. Releasing a value's quantum storage can precede clearing its measurement phase.

Two identities drive register reuse

Purpose. Derive the identities that allow the point-addition intermediates to overwrite existing coordinate registers.

For ordinary, nonexceptional inputs \(P=(x_P,y_P)\), \(Q=(x_Q,y_Q)\), set \(d_x=x_P-x_Q\), \(d_y=y_P-y_Q\), and \(\lambda=d_y/d_x\pmod p\). The affine sum obeys

\[x_R=\lambda^2-x_P-x_Q,\qquad y_R=\lambda(x_P-x_R)-y_P.\]

Rearrange these into the quantities the existing registers can compute:

\[d_x+3x_Q-\lambda^2=x_Q-x_R,\qquad\lambda(x_Q-x_R)=y_R+y_Q.\]

The register trace

Purpose. Track the register contents so each routing stage has a definite mathematical meaning.

StageFirst coordinate registerSecond coordinate register
Differences\(d_x\)\(d_y\)
Division\(d_x\)\(\lambda\)
Add \(3x_Q\), subtract square\(x_Q-x_R\)\(\lambda\)
Multiply\(x_Q-x_R\)\(y_R+y_Q\)
Remove offsets; negate first\(x_R\)\(y_R\)

1. Lookup, subtract, release

Purpose. Load table coordinates only long enough to form differences, then release them for the next arithmetic stage.

The 16-bit table index stays live. Lookup places the selected coordinate next to its accumulator coordinate; subtraction creates a difference. X-measuring a spent table value frees its positions while recording a phase mask. Independent coordinate operations can overlap if their dependencies are respected.

2. Divide while the workspace changes shape

Purpose. Use the space freed by shrinking gcd operands to hold other data and the compressed branch record.

Binary-gcd registers occupy the U/V lane. As they shrink, released positions hold another operand and compressed history. The slope replaces \(d_y\); replaying the recorded computation restores clean work. Peak demand is 68 active blocks plus one index block.

3. Compute the new x coordinate indirectly

Purpose. Compute the new coordinate indirectly so the square-subtract stage can reuse the existing registers.

Lookup \(3x_Q\), add it to \(d_x\), and subtract \(\lambda^2\). Shifts of the square product also perform useful alignment. Algorithm 6 adds and later removes a random field mask \(R_{\rm mask}\) around this sequence: it cancels algebraically but is essential to the failure bound.

4. Reuse the large workspace for multiplication

Purpose. Reuse the division workspace for multiplication instead of allocating another large arithmetic region.

Pack the inactive register; place the active operands in the lane. Multiplication turns the slope into \(y_R+y_Q\), then clears its gcd history. The same work region has now served both division and multiplication.

5. Remove offsets and accumulated lookup phases

Purpose. Remove remaining coordinate offsets and measurement phases before returning to the window’s entry layout.

Final coordinate lookups supply the offsets. For table index \(j\), let \(f(j)\) be the loaded coordinate bit string and \(m_1,m_2\) its X-readout masks. Binary inner products give phases; repeated lookups combine by XOR:

\[(-1)^{m_1\cdot f(j)}(-1)^{m_2\cdot f(j)}=(-1)^{(m_1\oplus m_2)\cdot f(j)}.\]

The phase-fix lookup clears these records, including the separate \(3x_Q\) mask. Packing restores the entry arrangement.

Closing the layout makes component costs composable

Purpose. Show why restoring the layout lets separately compiled component costs compose without an uncounted relocation step.

The authored placement path supports the conservative allowance of 20 additional layers per window when combining separately compiled components. It is a logical execution plan under the architecture model.
summary: This appendix makes the routing claim concrete for one full point addition. It tracks both register values and their locations, showing how workspace is reused and how the final layout permits the next window to begin.
title: Appendix C · Follow one point-addition window through memory

body:
The run configuration is part of the result

Purpose. State the configuration choices needed to determine a compiled schedule rather than treating compilation as a unique mapping.

A component is a reversible quantum map with named input, output, and clean-work registers. Lowering replaces it by smaller implementations until each operation is supported by the hardware. A Clifford frame stores unapplied Clifford gates and updates later measurement questions.

The compiler consumes a root component, parameters, architecture, layout plan, and synthesis options. It emits a measurement schedule and metrics. The architecture declares memory geometry, legal operations, concurrency, and factory preparation/cleanup. A layer count cannot be reproduced from the arithmetic map alone.

1. Lower until every leaf is legal

Purpose. Expand abstract operations until the remaining instructions are supported by the target architecture.

Choose a definition

An abstract adder becomes a selected carry circuit.

Bind its work

Map operands and temporary qubits into the planned blocks.

Check each child

Keep legal measurements and frame updates; decompose the rest.

Each substitution must preserve its public map and clean-work contract. Induction over validated substitutions preserves the root operation. Cross-block support must become legal during this process.

2. Retain repeated structure during lowering

Purpose. Retain repeated structure instead of eagerly duplicating the full circuit during every lowering stage.

Let \(L\) count iterations and \(V_i\) be the operation in iteration \(i\). A loop stores one body and an iteration-dependent binding \(\theta_i\), such as a bit slice, width, or constant. Its final execution remains

\[U=V_{L-1}(\theta_{L-1})\cdots V_0(\theta_0).\]

Inversion reverses the execution order

Purpose. Show why reversing a repeated operation also reverses its execution order.

Forward executionInverse execution
\(V_0,\ V_1,\ V_2\)\(V_2^\dagger,\ V_1^\dagger,\ V_0^\dagger\)

Reusing a loop body saves compilation work; every scheduled operation still executes. Width and operand bindings can change at each iteration.

3. Cache structure, remap local outcomes

Purpose. Reuse compiled structure safely by giving copied measurements fresh local identities.

Matching component types, parameters, selected definitions, and compatible work bindings can reuse a lowered subtree. Measurement identities must be fresh for each occurrence:

First occurrenceReplayed occurrence
Measure work \(\to m_1\); correct using \(m_1\)Measure work \(\to m_2\); correct using \(m_2\)

Reusing \(m_1\) in the second correction changes the program. Replay also preserves ownership and factory-loan bookkeeping; changed context invalidates the cache. Reused decompositions are scheduled anew.

4. Allocate states when timing is known

Purpose. Assign factory outputs only when the schedule determines when each resource state is needed.

Factory qubits remain virtual during lowering. The scheduler draws from an available-state pool on injection and restores capacity at the matching cleanup. With consistent within-layer timing,

\[A_{\ell+1}=A_\ell-I_\ell+C_\ell,\qquad0\le A_\ell\le R.\]

Here \(A_\ell\) is available capacity, \(I_\ell\) injections, \(C_\ell\) completed cleanups, and \(R\) pool capacity. Actual preparation readiness and the one-injection-per-layer limit still apply. Each CCZ injection couples its three resource qubits to data through three ZZ measurements. Physical factory assignments are resolved after scheduling.

5. Store the long schedule compactly

Purpose. Represent a very long schedule compactly without changing its operations or dependencies.

Block-local Pauli masks and flat instruction arrays avoid heavyweight objects for hundreds of millions of measurements. This changes compiler memory use, not execution cost.

6. Encode the placement insight explicitly

Purpose. Make placement choices explicit so arithmetic structure can guide routing rather than leaving it entirely to generic search.

The adder lane maps bit \(i\) to block \(\lfloor i/7\rfloor\), with operand/work slots \(3(i\bmod7)+\{0,1,2\}\); slot 21 is the relay. Such plans supply algorithmic design knowledge while the compiler handles legal decomposition and timing. They therefore belong in the reproducible run description.
summary: This appendix describes how the compiler preserves structure while constructing a long measurement schedule. Explicit configuration, scoped measurement records and delayed resource assignment make the compiled result interpretable and reproducible.
title: Appendix D · How the hierarchy becomes a concrete schedule

body:
From a small LUT to the circuit IonQ uses

Purpose. Build the lookup from defined small circuits before explaining IonQ’s routing and parallel schedule.

A lookup table is a classical list of words \(D_t\in\{0,1\}^m\), compiled into gates. Its quantum contract is \(|j,y\rangle\mapsto|j,y\oplus D_j\rangle\). Here j is the address; y is an output bit string, not specifically the elliptic curve’s y-coordinate. Read the following circuits in order: a controlled one-bit lookup, its recursive extension, then the paper’s parallel scheduling and cleanup.

1. One nonlinear test controls an entire word

Purpose. Compute one nonlinear selector and reuse it across an entire classical word and both address branches.

Introduce an enable qubit c. The desired map is \(y\mapsto y\oplus cD_x\), where x is one address bit. First compute \(a=cx\), and use a to XOR-load \(D_1\). A CNOT from c then changes \(a\) to \(cx\oplus c=c(1-x)\), which enables the \(D_0\) load. Another CNOT restores \(a=cx\) for cleanup:

\[y_{\rm out}=y\oplus cxD_1\oplus c(1-x)D_0=y\oplus cD_x.\]

Each word load is a collection of CNOTs; the nonlinear cost is one AND, independent of word width. Increasing m still increases output qubits, Clifford gates and communication. The X measurement gives phase \((-1)^{\mu cx}\); conditional CZ contributes the same sign and cancels it. There is no second AND computation for cleanup.

2. Replace each word load with a smaller lookup

Purpose. Extend the one-bit circuit recursively without repeating full address tests for every output bit.

For address \(x_1x_0\), split the table into \((D_{00},D_{01})\) and \((D_{10},D_{11})\). Replace each mask box by the one-bit circuit above, enabled by the current a. This computes \(y\mapsto y\oplus cD_{x_1x_0}\).

There is one AND for the branch split and one in each child: three total. The circuit visits both children in a fixed sequence. A zero selector disables a child on a basis branch; it does not mean the quantum computer measures the branch or skips its gates.

3. An entire eight-entry LUT, with every box defined

Purpose. Assemble a complete eight-entry lookup from the defined subcircuits and account for its temporary storage.

For example, on j=101 the first half is disabled; the second half selects its row 01, so the output is \(y\oplus D_{101}\). On a superposition of addresses, the same fixed circuit performs all corresponding branches coherently. The three drawings together specify the complete construction for arbitrary eight m-bit words.

This recursive execution is called unary iteration: successive work qubits encode predicates such as “the address begins with 10.” It does not store all \(2^k\) selectors simultaneously. A depth-first traversal retains O(k) prefix work qubits, reusing them when it returns from a subtree.

\[C_0=0,\qquad C_k=1+2C_{k-1}=2^k-1,\qquad U_k=2C_{k-1}=2^k-2\quad(k\ge1).\]

Here C counts AND computations in a controlled k-bit lookup and U in an uncontrolled one. Thus an eight-entry lookup uses six AND computations in this construction. For 16 address bits, \(U_{16}=65{,}534\). These are logical construction counts, not the full routed layer count of IonQ’s lookup.

4. The paper: split 16 address bits into two controlled 15-bit traversals

Purpose. Overlap two controlled half-table traversals to keep shared output resources busy; the table’s logical contents remain unchanged.

Write \(j=(h,\ell)\), with one high bit h and 15 lower bits ℓ. The two tables are \(D^{(0)}_\ell=D_{0\ell}\) and \(D^{(1)}_\ell=D_{1\ell}\). Their enabled XOR maps commute:

\[y\longmapsto y\oplus(1-h)D^{(0)}_\ell\oplus hD^{(1)}_\ell=y\oplus D_j.\]

IonQ follows the zipper construction of Ref. [68], §4.1 and Figs. 10–11: give the two halves separate address copies and prefix work, overlap their private operations, and alternate their writes into the common output. The three-bit version makes that order visible:

The second traversal can prepare its next selector while the first writes. Both do not write a shared target qubit at the same instant. Zipper improves scheduling at a cost in workspace; it does not remove half the table entries or halve the nonlinear gate count by itself. The source reference’s surface-code cycle estimates are not the IonQ timing model.

5. How IonQ distributes a selected row across code blocks

Purpose. Make wide writes compatible with code-block locality by relaying selectors and clearing their temporary copies.

In the IonQ paper, §IX D (“Lookup,” p. 18), scratch qubits and the lowest index bit share a memory block so traversal CNOTs stay local. Relevant higher index bits are copied into that block for CCZ injections, then their copies are cleared. A selector is relayed to output blocks to apply each block’s portion of the table word. Here is one such block:

The zipper version adds index copies and a second relay qubit in each target block, supporting the two traversals. These are entangled computational-basis copies, not independent copies of an unknown state. Actual routing uses the paper’s copy/fanout and measurement-based uncomputation primitives. Integrated routing explains how the block operations enter the schedule.

Yes: measurements replace coherent uncomputation

Purpose. Replace coherent inverse computation with measurement, reset and feedforward, while proving that all input coherence is restored.

Ordinarily, running the inverse lookup would implement \(|j,F(j)\rangle\mapsto|j,0\rangle\). Measurement-based uncomputation instead measures the temporary output in the X basis, resets those qubits, and repairs the phase on the retained address. All measurement outcomes are accepted: there is no postselection.

To see why this preserves an arbitrary coherent input, include the rest of the computer as \(|\psi_j\rangle\):

\[|\Psi\rangle=\sum_j\alpha_j|j\rangle|F(j)\rangle|\psi_j\rangle,\qquad \sum_j|\alpha_j|^2=1.\]

For b measured bits, \(\langle m|H^{\otimes b}|F(j)\rangle=2^{-b/2}(-1)^{m\cdot F(j)}\). Orthogonality of the retained addresses then gives \(\Pr(m)=2^{-b}\), independent of the address distribution. Conditioned on the recorded m, the normalized remaining state is

\[|\Psi_m\rangle=\sum_j\alpha_j(-1)^{m\cdot F(j)}|j\rangle|\psi_j\rangle.\]

The outcome tells us no address information, but it specifies a phase error. Apply \(D_m\), and the two signs multiply to +1 for every j, recovering \(\sum_j\alpha_j|j\rangle|\psi_j\rangle\). A computational-basis measurement directly on F(j) would instead distinguish addresses with different table values and could not be repaired by this phase correction.

Recording m matters. If we discard the result without correction, averaging over m suppresses coherence between j and j′ whenever \(F(j)\ne F(j')\). Measurement alone is not cleanup; measurement, reset, and the recorded phase correction together implement cleanup.

Measured temporary valueInduced phaseRequired correction
Copied bit a\((-1)^{\mu a}\)\(Z^\mu\) on a
AND ab\((-1)^{\mu ab}\)\(CZ^\mu\) on a,b
Lookup word F(j)\((-1)^{m\cdot F(j)}\)Generally nonlinear phase lookup on j

The first two corrections are Clifford operations. The last is not generally Clifford or a Pauli-frame update. Its cost must be included: freeing a wide register does not make its phase correction free.

6. Free the loaded coordinates without measuring the address

Purpose. Repair the generally nonlinear address phase left by measuring a coordinate word; this correction is not automatically a Pauli update.

Two cleanups must be distinguished. Erasing a temporary AND uses the simple CZ correction above. Erasing a full coordinate word F(j) requires a generally nonlinear phase function of the address:

\[\sum_j\alpha_j|j,F(j)\rangle\xrightarrow{M_X(B)=m}\sum_j\alpha_j(-1)^{m\cdot F(j)}|j\rangle.\]

For known measurement mask m, compute the one-bit classical table \(g_m(t)=m\cdot F(t)\pmod2\). Its phase lookup cancels that sign:

The address remains coherent and unmeasured. Arithmetic controlled by j can continue while the phase correction is deferred. For the three point-addition lookups, the exact correction table combines the readout masks:

\[g(j)=(m_x^{(1)}\oplus m_x^{(3)})\cdot x_j\;\oplus\;(m_y^{(1)}\oplus m_y^{(3)})\cdot y_j\;\oplus\;m_{3x}^{(2)}\cdot (3x_j\bmod p).\]

Inner products here use coordinate bit strings. The labels xⱼ,yⱼ are table coordinates. The paper’s Algorithm 6 accumulates these masks and ends with LookupPhaseFix. Appendix E explicitly says its compiled phase-fix is suboptimal and does not implement Ref. [22]’s phaseup optimization; the one-bit contract above should not be read as an extra optimization already included in its totals.

Sources: IonQ paper §IX D, p. 18, Algorithm 6 and Appendix E; Ref. [68], §2 (recursive lookup) and §4.1 (zipper). The drawings expand the logical mechanisms and distinguish them from physical measurement schedules.

A copied address is an entangled control

Purpose. Distribute or move a computational-basis control coherently, then erase the spare carrier with a simple phase correction.

\[\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle\longmapsto\alpha|00\rangle+\beta|11\rangle.\]

The copies distribute a computational-basis control. X-measuring a spare address register with outcome mask \(m\) leaves phase \((-1)^{m\cdot x}\), canceled by the corresponding Z gates on the retained register. The circuit below instead erases the original, completing a move.
